title: Key-Search Attacks Bypass Encrypted Activation Monitors

contributions.purpose: Show that key-conditioned embedding obfuscation lets adversaries evade activation-based safety monitors.
contributions.mechanism: Key-search attack: a malicious client samples K encryption keys for the same harmful prompt, runs each through the encryptor and frozen transformer, and submits the version whose server-side monitor score is minimized (below threshold).
contributions.evaluation: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with an OSNIP-style encryptor, reduces monitor TPR from 84.9% to 59.9% at K=64 (25.0pp drop) and to 16.2% at K=512 (68.6pp drop) at FPR=1e-3; encryption alone at K=1 leaves TPR unchanged.
contributions.domain: LLM safety / privacy-preserving split inference (activation monitoring)
contributions.source_quote: we demonstrate that key-search attacks significantly degrade encrypted activation monitors, reducing TPR from 84.9% to 59.9% at K=64 (25.0pp drop) and to 16.2% at K=512 (68.6pp drop) at FPR=1e-3.

contributions.purpose: Establish that key diversity is the necessary condition for attack effectiveness.
contributions.mechanism: Ablate the key-diversity training loss (lambda2=0.5 vs 0) and correlate per-prompt score variance across keys with bypass probability.
contributions.evaluation: Without diversity, TPR drops only 5.0pp at K=64 vs 25.0pp with high diversity (5x difference); bypassed prompts have 5x higher score variance (0.020 vs 0.004), r=0.458, p<1e-13.
contributions.source_quote: we show that key diversity is essential for attack effectiveness: without diversity regularization, TPR drops by only 5.0pp at K=64 compared to 25.0pp with high diversity, a 5x difference.

contributions.purpose: Reveal a fundamental tradeoff constraining whether OSNIP-like schemes can be both private and attack-resistant.
contributions.mechanism: Compare encryptor configurations on key diversity, utility (KL divergence), and privacy (inversion ASR@10) against target constraints.
contributions.evaluation: High-diversity encryptor enabling effective attacks violates utility (KL=0.031 vs target 0.02) and privacy (ASR@10=0.526 vs target 0.20); the standard low-diversity encryptor meets both but resists attacks (only 5.0pp drop at K=64).
contributions.source_quote: we reveal a utility-privacy-diversity tradeoff: effective attacks require high key diversity that violates both utility (KL divergence) and privacy (inversion attack success rate) constraints, suggesting that well-designed OSNIP-like schemes may resist key-search attacks.

self_declared_provenance.quote: We train a key-conditioned encryptor following the OSNIP framework (Cao et al., 2026) with three loss components.
Our key-search attack shares this sampling-based strategy but operates in the embedding space rather than prompt space.
Following prior work on activation monitoring (Patel & Wang), we train an MLP probe on layer-l activations to classify harmful versus harmless requests.
OSNIP (Cao et al., 2026) proposes key-conditioned obfuscation that projects embeddings into a semantic null space ... These methods assume honest users; we study adversarial key selection.

notes: Contains an internal tension framed as a tradeoff: attack is strong only under high key diversity, which itself violates utility and privacy constraints, so well-designed low-diversity OSNIP schemes are largely resistant (only ~5pp drop).
